metadata.file_name: 210. Kuang (2026). Evaluating Neural Networks Architectures for Competency Prediction from Process Data Using PISA Computer-Based Mathematics Assessment.pdf
metadata.title: Evaluating Neural Networks Architectures for Competency Prediction from Process Data Using PISA Computer-Based Mathematics Assessment

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the U.S. sample from the PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics assessment (CBMA) and restricts the analytic dataset to 402 students with complete action-sequence data for the specified CBMA units/items. The paper reports item-level sample sizes (378–402) and uses complete data across all ten items for the assessment-level model (n=376), but it does not report applying PISA complex survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the analysis is based on neural-network models (RNN/GRU/LSTM) trained with TensorFlow and evaluated via student-level stratified cross-validation, the manuscript does not describe weight-aware estimation; this suggests an unweighted ML pipeline. The main preprocessing described is sequence padding with zeros to equalize sequence lengths per item and student-level fold splitting to prevent leakage.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the publicly available PISA 2012 CBMA process-data dataset for the U.S. sample. The study draws on 402 U.S. students for item-level models, with item-level sample sizes reduced (378–402) due to missing or invalid responses. For the assessment-level latent proficiency model, only students with complete data across all ten items were retained (n=376, 95%). Sequential inputs were constructed from action sequences for the ten CBMA items and padded with zeros to a fixed maximum sequence length per item; cross-validation splitting was performed at the student level to avoid student-level leakage.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Computer-Based Mathematics Assessment (CBMA) — U.S. sample (item-level correctness; 10 CBMA items across CM015, CM020, CM038)
main_findings.performance_metrics: AUC: average >0.6 for most items; exception CM038Q06 ~0.5. Cohen’s Kappa: average >0.25 for most items; exception CM038Q06 ~0.0. Expert-engineered features: slightly higher AUC across most conditions; minor Kappa changes; training time generally reduced when adding expert-engineered features.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 CBMA U.S. process-the study leveraged expert-engineered process summaries (e.g., total response time, time before first attempt, total number of events) together with action-sequence inputs to predict item-level correctness, finding that adding expert-engineered features produced only small AUC/Kappa gains but generally reduced training time. This indicates that for item-level prediction in CBMA tasks, simpler sequence-only neural models may be sufficient for accuracy, while expert features mainly help computational efficiency and interpretability rather than substantially improving discrimination.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Computer-Based Mathematics Assessment (CBMA) — U.S. sample (assessment-level latent proficiency; PV1 from 30-item mathematics assessment; predicted from 10 CBMA items)
main_findings.target_variable: Assessment-level latent proficiency (PISA plausible value PV1; correlation and RMSE)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlation (Pearson r) between predicted latent proficiency and PV1: 0.28–0.62 depending on architecture and feature set. Largest improvement with expert-engineered features: two-layer LSTM with 100 nodes correlation increased from 0.36 to 0.62. RMSE: expert-engineered features generally lowered RMSE (e.g., one-layer RNN with 100 nodes 1.16→0.93) with some GRU exceptions. Training time increased when adding expert-engineered features (e.g., one-layer RNN 50 nodes 46.77s→130.09s; one-layer LSTM 50 nodes 94.34s→1189.32s).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 CBMA U.S. process-the study leveraged action sequences and expert-engineered process features to predict assessment-level latent proficiency (PV1), finding that adding expert-engineered features improved predictive accuracy (correlation up to r=0.62) and reduced RMSE across most architectures, while increasing training time. This indicates that combining sequential behavior with domain-informed process summaries can strengthen early proficiency estimation from a limited item subset, supporting adaptive testing designs that trade some computational cost for better measurement precision.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses the U.S. sample from the PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics assessment (CBMA) process-data to train recurrent neural networks (RNN, GRU, LSTM) that predict (i) item-level correctness and (ii) assessment-level latent proficiency. Item-level models are evaluated with AUC and Cohen’s Kappa, showing good discrimination for most items (AUC mostly >0.6; Kappa mostly >0.25) with CM038Q06 near chance (AUC ~0.5; Kappa ~0). Assessment-level models predict PV1 (single plausible value) from action sequences of 10 CBMA items and are evaluated with Pearson correlation and RMSE; correlations range from 0.28 to 0.62, with the best result for a two-layer LSTM with 100 nodes when expert-engineered features are included. Adding expert-engineered features generally improves accuracy (and interpretability via SHAP) but increases training time, and architectural complexity beyond simple configurations yields little benefit. Limitations include an unweighted ML pipeline (no survey-weight discussion) and the use of SHAP for feature importance rather than causal inference.
